newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy warned it might miss key EMU target.
newsitem.headline: Italy warned it might miss key EMU target.

text.p: The European Commission and International Monetary Fund warned Italy on Wednesday that it might fail in its strenuous bid to make the grade for the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
But while the Washington-based IMF said that France and Germany also risked falling short of the mark, the European Commission said only Italy and Greece were in danger of failure.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who has pledged to resign if Italy misses the EMU boat, slammed the Commission figures and accused Brussels of not taking into account the available data.

"The Commission's decision to forecast at this stage a financial unbalance, albeit minimal, in a member state that has already taken necessary and correct steps to cut the deficit...is incomprehensible," Prodi said in a statement.

The Commission predicted that the ratio between Italy's budget deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) would hit 3.2 percent this year and 3.9 percent in 1998, compared with the three percent target laid down by the Maastricht Treaty.

By contrast it forecast that both France and Germany would comply with the terms of the treaty. The IMF said that all three countries were heading for a 3.3 percent deficit/GDP ratio without further budget action.
Soothing words from the Commission that Italy might meet the Maastricht goal if recent budget action was fully effective did little to appease the anger of Prodi's centre-left allies.

"This (report) is a sign of prejudice against Italy rather than a serious financial analysis," said Lanfranco Turci, the economic spokesman for the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the largest party within Prodi's coalition.

Both the IMF and Commission indicated that Italy had introduced too many one-off budget measures in its drive to be among the first wave of countries signing up to the single European currency, scheduled for launch in 1999.

"In the absence of additional measures (this will) lead to a rebound of the deficit in subsequent years," the IMF warned, calling on the government to initiate structural spending cuts to the welfare state.

Prodi, who has already pledged to launch a review of social spending, said Italy will have met key Maastricht goals by the time European Union leaders gather in May 1998 to decide the starting line-up for the single currency.

"The government...is deeply committed to following its own action of structural reform which will enable Italy to arrive at the single currency date with all its papers in order," Prodi's statement said.

Italy, burdened by a huge debt mountain, had a deficit/GDP ratio of 6.7 percent in 1996 and the government has introduced deficit-cutting measures worth some 78 trillion lire ($45.8 billion) over the past four months to meet EMU targets.
Financial markets were little moved by the flurry of forecasts, but the hard-right National Alliance said the figures showed Prodi coalition was on the wrong track.
"Italy will only enter Europe if it changes its economic policy, which means changing the government majority," National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini told reporters.

The hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's parliamentary majority, said the Commission had ignored Italy's true economic performance and was seeking to force the government into a radical overhaul of the welfare state.
"(The Commission) is exerting the most violent pressure on Italy to make it go down the wrong road and cut the welfare state," Bertinotti said. ($1 = 1,700 lire)
